dedupe_keys.name: ijkdijk full scale levee failure and sensor validation tests netherlands 2008 2012

description: The IJkdijk ("calibration dike") was a Dutch test site near Groningen where full-scale levees were built and deliberately brought to failure, to learn how dikes fail and to test sensor systems for flood early warning under field conditions. The programme ran from 2008 to 2014 with Deltares coordinating tests and many sensor and data companies taking part. A macro-stability test in 2008 showed deformation starting 42 hours before the breach at the exact point of collapse; four piping (underseepage erosion) experiments in 2009 produced the first observed piping collapse of a dike and showed that a drain in the right place prevents it; and the 2012 All-in-One Sensor Validation Test failed two basin dikes by internal overtopping on 26 and 27 August and a third by sliding on 8 September, while sensors measured pore pressure, soil temperature (including infrared cameras and fibre optics) and soil movement, shown on live dashboards. Results are documented in papers (de Vries, Koelewijn and Hopman, ASCE 2010), a Wageningen report on smart levees and news from Dutch Water Sector; the programme site is offline, no raw sensor dataset was found openly published, and the reports are free to read except the paywalled ASCE paper, with no licence stated. Caveats: sites and soils are specific to the Groningen tests, and some reports are paywalled. Simulation uses: calibration and validation of levee failure mechanisms, breach timing and sensor-based early warning or digital-twin systems for flood defences. Related records: the US National Levee Database (data-usace-national-levee-database), England's AIMS flood defences (data-ea-aims-spatial-flood-defences) and the worldwide dam failures database (data-worldwide-historical-dam-failures-database).

outcomes: Full-scale test levees were brought to failure: in 2008 deformation started 42 hours before the breach exactly where it occurred, the 2009 piping tests showed piping leading to collapse and that a well-placed drain can prevent it, and in 2012 soil movement sensors registered lateral movement four days before a breach.
